2.2 for loops
Repeat a block a fixed number of times: the body runs once per value:

A simple for loop
for (i in 1:5) print(i^2)            # i takes each value of the sequence in turn
total <- 0                           # the body runs once per value
for (x in c(2, 4, 6, 8)) total <- total + x
total   # 20


Afterwards i is a normal variable: it still holds the loop’s last value.

2.3 Pre-allocate for speed
Growing a vector inside a loop is slow. Pre-allocate the result first:

Pre-allocate, then fill by index
n <- 1000
out <- numeric(n)          # a vector of n zeros, ready to fill
for (i in 1:n) {
  out[i] <- rnorm(1)
}


Rule of thumb. Decide the output’s length before the loop, create the container, then fill slots by index (out[i] <- ...). This is much faster than out <- c(out, ...) inside the loop, a habit that matters once your data grows.

2.4 while loops
Repeat while a condition holds: useful when you don’t know the number of steps in advance:

A while loop
x <- 1
while (x < 1000) {
  x <- x * 2
}
x    # 1024








Guard against infinite loops


If the condition never becomes FALSE, the loop runs forever. Always make sure something inside the body moves toward stopping the loop.

2.5 Conditionals: if / else if / else
Branch on a condition: only one branch runs:

if/else is an expression: it hands a value back
score <- 82
grade <- if (score >= 90) "A"
         else if (score >= 80) "B"
         else "C"








Long vectors break if


if needs a single TRUE/FALSE: use ifelse() for vectors.

2.6 Element-wise choice: ifelse
For vectorised decisions, use ifelse(condition, when_true, when_false):

Element-wise choice with ifelse
temps <- c(-2, 15, 28, 33)
ifelse(temps > 25, "hot", "not hot")

It applies the branch element-wise to a whole vector: no loop needed. This is the idiomatic replacement for “for each value, choose one of two things”.

if vs ifelse. Use if/else to choose which block of code runs once; use ifelse to map a vector to one of two values. Mixing them up is a classic beginner bug.

2.7 Which tool when?

for: repeat a block a known number of times (fill a pre-allocated vector, iterate over columns).
while: repeat until a condition flips (unknown count of steps).
if/else: choose one block of code based on a condition.
ifelse: map a vector element-wise to one of two values.
*apply family: “loop over each element and apply a function” (met in Session 1 with lists, and again below with matrices).


Often the cleanest loop is no loop at all: vectorization, ifelse, or lapply/vapply are simpler than an explicit for.

::: {.spread .spread-md .spread-evenly}
**`for`**: repeat a block a *known* number of times (fill a pre-allocated vector, iterate over columns).

**`while`**: repeat *until a condition* flips (unknown count of steps).

**`if/else`**: choose *one block of code* based on a condition.

**`ifelse`**: map a *vector* element-wise to one of two values.

**`*apply` family**: "loop over each element and apply a function" (met in Session 1 with lists, and again below with matrices).
:::

2.8 The *apply family: loop & apply
Say “apply this function to every element” instead of writing the loop by hand:

lapply, sapply, vapply
l <- list(a = 1:3, b = 4:6)
lapply(l, mean)          # a list back — keeps the original structure
sapply(l, mean)          # tries to simplify: a named vector
vapply(l, mean, 0)       # like sapply, but you promise the output type


The family you first met on lists in Session 1 (and will meet again on matrices as apply, MARGIN = …): lapply always, sapply when simple, vapply when you want the guarantee. It’s “loop, then apply” collapsed into one verb.

2.9 Grouped summaries in base R
group_by |> summarise (Session 2) has a base-R cousin that returns the split-by-group result directly:

tapply & aggregate, base R
tapply(penguins$body_mass_g, penguins$species, mean, na.rm = TRUE)
#   Adelie Chinstrap   Gentoo
#  3700.7    3733.1    5076.0

aggregate(body_mass_g ~ species, data = penguins, FUN = mean)


tapply(vector, group, fun) summarises by group; aggregate(formula, data, fun) returns a tidy data.frame. When your pipeline gets more steps, reach for the dplyr verbs; when it’s one grouped summary, these one-liners are hard to beat.

3.1 What is a matrix?
A matrix is a two-dimensional rectangular array of one type (usually numeric): a vector folded into rows and columns. It’s the 2D cousin of the vector.

Build and subset a matrix
m <- matrix(1:12, nrow = 3, ncol = 4)   # vector -> rows & columns
m[2, 3]      # subset with [row, col], like a data frame
dim(m)       # 3 4
nrow(m); ncol(m)   # 3 4


Key distinction. A data frame is a list of columns (columns may differ in type); a matrix is one vector in 2D (single type). For tabular data with mixed types, prefer a data frame/tibble; reach for a matrix when you need linear algebra.

3.2 Building & reshaping
A matrix is just a vector with a dim (dimension) attribute, so you can build or reshape them freely:

matrix(), rbind/cbind, and dim()
A <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 2, ncol = 3)          # column-major fill
identical(A, rbind(1:3, 4:6))                 # TRUE — cbind/rbind by row
cbind(A, c(7, 8))                             # add a column
dim(A) <- NULL                                # strip the dim -> back to a vector








Column-major by default


matrix() fills column by column unless you pass byrow = TRUE. A classic source of “why is my matrix transposed?” surprises.

3.3 Arithmetic & recycling
Element-wise arithmetic works like it does on vectors, and recycling applies:

Arithmetic on a matrix
M <- matrix(1:6, 2, 3)
M * 2            # scalar multiplies every entry
M + c(10, 20)    # length-2 vector recycles down the COLUMNS
M * matrix(c(1, 10), 2, 1)   # column vector scales each column


Watch the recycling axis. A length-2 vector recycles along columns (down), not across: get this wrong and your standardisation silently miscalculates each column.

3.4 Linear algebra
Matrices exist to do algebra: matrix product, transpose, inverse, determinant:

Matrix algebra
A <- matrix(c(2, 4, 1, 3), nrow = 2)   # a 2x2
A %*% A        # matrix product       t(A) # transpose
solve(A)       # inverse              det(A) # determinant
diag(4)        # 4x4 identity








%*% is not *


A * B is element-wise; A %*% B is the matrix product (rows × columns). Absent the right dimensions, %*% errors, which is usually the clue you wanted a matrix, not a data frame.

3.5 Fold a data frame into a matrix
Any rectangular numeric block can be coerced to a matrix when algebra needs it:

as.matrix() for numeric tables
nums <- iris[, 1:4]            # 150 x 4, all numeric
M    <- as.matrix(nums)        # data frame -> matrix
dim(M)                         # 150 4
class(M)                       # "matrix" "array"


as.matrix() forces everything to one type: if any column is character, the whole matrix becomes character. Check str() before you coerce, and keep a real data frame for mixed-type data.

3.6 Row/column summaries & apply
Summarise along one axis with the row*/col* helpers, or generalise with apply:

rowSums, colMeans, and apply(MARGIN)
M <- matrix(1:12, 3, 4)
rowSums(M); rowMeans(M)     # per row   (MARGIN = 1)
colSums(M); colMeans(M)     # per column (MARGIN = 2)
apply(M, 1, sd)             # sd of each row
apply(M, 2, function(x) max(x) - min(x))   # range of each column


apply(M, MARGIN, fun): MARGIN = 1 goes down rows, MARGIN = 2 across columns. It’s lapply’s 2D sibling: a loop over one axis hidden inside a one-liner.

```r
colSums(M); colMeans(M)     # per column (MARGIN = 2)
apply(M, 1, sd)             # sd of each row
apply(M, 2, function(x) max(x) - min(x))   # range of each column
```
:::

3.7 Standardise a matrix (full example)
Let’s z-score every column of a matrix, the machinery behind a real analysis:

Column-wise z-scoring
M   <- matrix(c(1, 100, 2, 200), 2, 2)
mu  <- colMeans(M)            # mean of each column
sig <- apply(M, 2, sd)        # sd of each column
Z   <- sweep(M, 2, mu, "-")   # subtract each column's mean
Z   <- sweep(Z, 2, sig, "/")  # divide each column's sd
colMeans(Z)                   # ~ 0
apply(Z, 2, sd)               # ~ 1


sweep(M, MARGIN, vector, FUN) applies a function across one axis, here subtracting a column mean. This is the pattern scale(M) automates; you now see what’s underneath.

4.3 Scope: what the body sees
Variables created inside a function live only there: they don’t leak out:

What the body sees
g <- function(x) {
  internal <- x * 2    # exists only inside the call
  internal + 1
}
g(5)          # 11








Lexical scoping


A function can see variables from the outside, but relying on that is fragile: pass everything it needs as arguments. Explicit inputs in, explicit output out, is what makes functions testable and reusable.

Functions are vectorised: they work element-wise on vectors:

Vectorised with defaults
f_to_c(c(32, 212, 98.6))   # works on the whole vector

ifelse in the body: the element-wise tool from earlier, and the vectorised clamp needs no loop at all.

4.6 When functions aren’t vectorised: Vectorize() & replicate()
Built-in functions are usually vectorised, but your own (or a third-party) function may only accept one scalar at a time. Two loop-free helpers:

Vectorize() wraps a scalar function so it takes a vector; replicate() repeats an expression
# not vectorised: takes one date string
parse_it <- function(x) strsplit(x, "-")[[1]][1]
parse_it(c("2024-05-01", "2024-06-15"))   # only the first is parsed

parse_all <- Vectorize(parse_it)          # wraps it => element-wise
parse_all(c("2024-05-01", "2024-06-15"))

set.seed(7)
replicate(4, mean(rexp(10)))              # repeat an expression R times


Loops without loops. Vectorize() turns a scalar-only function into a vector one; replicate(R, expr) re-runs an expression R times and collects results, the function-flavoured cousin of for/sapply. Works with any expression, not just a named function.


markdown## When functions aren't vectorised: `Vectorize()` & `replicate()` {.inv}

4.8 Test your functions
A good habit: check a function against a case you already know the answer to:

One-line assertions with stopifnot
stopifnot(f_to_c(32) == 0)         # freezing
stopifnot(f_to_c(212) == 100)      # boiling

Why it matters. Writing one-line assertions (stopifnot) turns “trust me” into “checked automatically”. You’ll build on this with a proper testing framework in the Reproducible Workflows course.

1.2 The R ecosystem

R centres on two complementary toolkits:


Base R: ships with every installation, so it needs zero setup (works offline, even in locked-down environments). Functions like mean(), plot(), c(), [. Powerful and always available, but its ergonomics date back decades.


The tidyverse: an opinionated collection of packages (dplyr, ggplot2, tidyr, readr) sharing one grammar. Install once, then library(tidyverse) loads them all. The default toolkit for modern data work.


In this course we start from base R so you understand the foundations, then lean on the tidyverse for day-to-day work.

3.9 Special values
R has its own vocabulary for edge cases:

NA: missing (“Not Available”). A hole in your data. x <- NA.
NaN: Not a Number, e.g. 0/0. A kind of missing numeric.
Inf: Infinity, e.g. 1/0. Overflow or divergence.
NULL: empty/absent. Means “no value here at all”, different from NA.


Anticipate missingness. NA is contagious: most functions on data containing NA return NA unless you say na.rm = TRUE. We’ll meet this again (and handle it properly) in the data-cleaning lab.

4.5 Subsetting atomic vectors
There are four ways to pick elements with [, grouped into the three kinds below, plus the mental model that unifies them:

PositiveNegativeLogicalCharacterThe key mental model



Positive

x <- c("one", "two", "three", "four", "five")
x[c(3, 2, 5)]   # keep by position

[1] "three" "two"   "five" 






Negative

x <- c("one", "two", "three", "four", "five")
x[c(-1, -3, -5)]   # drop by position, equivalent to

[1] "two"  "four"

x[-c(1, 3, 5)]

[1] "two"  "four"






Logical

x <- c(10, 3, NA, 5, 8, 1, NA)
x[!is.na(x)]

[1] 10  3  5  8  1

x[x %% 2 == 0]

[1] 10 NA  8 NA






Character

x[c("xyz", "def")]

xyz def 
  5   2 





x[selector] returns elements where the selector is TRUE: the logical form.

mental model

[1]  5 NA  8

markdown## Subsetting atomic vectors {.inv}

There are **four** ways to pick elements with `[`, grouped into the three kinds below, plus the mental model that unifies them:

::: {.panel-tabset}
### Positive
::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"}
Positive
```{r}
x <- c("one", "two", "three", "four", "five")
x[c(3, 2, 5)]   # keep by position
```
:::

### Negative
::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"}
Negative
```{r}
x <- c("one", "two", "three", "four", "five")
x[c(-1, -3, -5)]   # drop by position, equivalent to
x[-c(1, 3, 5)]
```
:::

### Logical
::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"}
Logical
```{r}
x <- c(10, 3, NA, 5, 8, 1, NA)
x[!is.na(x)]
x[x %% 2 == 0]
```
:::

### Character
::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"}
Character
```{r}
x <- c(abc = 1, def = 2, xyz = 5)
x[c("xyz", "def")]
```
:::

### The key mental model
`x[selector]` returns elements **where the selector is TRUE**: the **logical** form.

::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"}
mental model
```{r}
x <- c(5, 1, NA, 8, 2)
x[x > 3]        # "x, where x is greater than 3"
x[!is.na(x)]    # "x, where x is not missing"
```
:::

::: {.callout-desc}
**`NA` trap.** `x[x %% 2 == 0]` keeps `NA`s too: `NA %% 2 == 0` is `NA`.

5.2 Applying a function to every element
The *apply family does “for each element, run this function”:

lapply / sapply

my_list <- list(var1 = rnorm(n = 20L), var2 = runif(n = 12L), var3 = rbinom(n = 42L, size = 1, prob = 0.5))
lapply(my_list, FUN = mean)   # returns a list

$var1
[1] 0.1945664

$var2
[1] 0.4760063

$var3
[1] 0.6190476

sapply(my_list, FUN = mean)   # tries to simplify to an atomic vector

     var1      var2      var3 
0.1945664 0.4760063 0.6190476 




vapply for safety. vapply(my_list, mean, FUN.VALUE = numeric(1)) promises the output type up front and fails loudly: prefer it in code you ship.

macOS / Windows: https://cran.r-project.org

Quarto is our open-source scientific and technical publishing system. It turns .qmd documents (and RevealJS slides!) into polished HTML, PDF, and more.

Download: https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/

quarto --version   # e.g. 1.10.x

title: Setup your machine for data science with R & Python

3. Install Positron (the IDE)
Positron is a next-generation data science IDE (a data-science-flavoured fork of VS Code) that runs both R and Python.

Download: https://positron.posit.co/download.html

title: Setup your machine for data science with R & Python
text:
4. Linux (Ubuntu)
If you run Ubuntu, install the three applications above from their .deb binaries, then set up R packages. Two routes are available for packages: the fast, recommended r2u binaries, or a manual compile-from-source fallback. Both are detailed below.

4.1 Install R, Quarto and Positron from .deb files
Download the .deb installer for each of R, Quarto and Positron from their respective sites (choose the arm64 build on an ARM, Apple-Silicon-style machine, or x86_64 otherwise). Then install them together and let apt pull in any missing dependencies:
sudo dpkg -i ~/Downloads/*.deb     # adjust the path to where you saved the files
sudo apt --fix-broken install
The second command is the important clean-up step: dpkg -i itself does not install dependency packages, so it will often report missing dependencies, which apt --fix-broken install then resolves. If you prefer, a plain sudo apt install -f works the same.
For R alone you do not have to use the CRAN .deb at all. If you prefer your package manager, install r-base (and r-base-dev) from the Ubuntu or CRAN apt repository afterwards with sudo apt install r-base r-base-dev instead. Either way you do not need RStudio: Positron is the IDE, and it talks to whatever R binary sits on your PATH.


4.2 Recommended: install R packages via r2u (Ubuntu binaries)
r2u is a project that builds almost all of CRAN (currently about 25,000 packages) into Ubuntu binary .deb packages and serves them as an apt repository. With a small companion called bspm, your ordinary install.packages("tidyverse") transparently installs prebuilt Ubuntu binaries in seconds, with no compilation and no manual wiring of system libraries. This removes precisely the libcurl/fontconfig/harfbuzz… laundry list that makes a source install painful.
Scope and caveats:

It targets Ubuntu LTS releases (22.04 “jammy”, 24.04 “noble”, 26.04 “resolute”) on amd64, with arm64 supported on 24.04 and 26.04. It is not for other distributions.
Installing via bspm needs sudo: it writes into the system R library.
renv-based projects (used later in the Reproducible Workflows course) do not go through bspm; they compile from source. So keep the build tools from the fallback below even if you use r2u.

Set it up (condensed from the official guide):
# 1. fetch the signing key
sudo apt update
sudo apt install --yes --no-install-recommends wget ca-certificates gnupg
gpg --homedir /tmp --no-default-keyring \
    --keyring /usr/share/keyrings/r2u.gpg \
    --keyserver keyserver.ubuntu.com \
    --recv-keys A1489FE2AB99A21A 67C2D66C4B1D4339 51716619E084DAB9

# 2. register the r2u apt repository (adjust 'noble' to your Ubuntu release:
#    jammy, noble or resolute; use `lsb_release -cs` to print it)
echo "deb [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/r2u.gpg] https://r2u.stat.illinois.edu/ubuntu noble main" \
    | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/r2u.list
sudo apt update

# 3. python pieces bspm needs, then bspm itself
sudo apt install --yes --no-install-recommends python3-{dbus,gi,apt}
sudo Rscript -e 'install.packages("bspm")'

# 4. enable bspm for every R session
sudo bash -c 'echo "suppressMessages(bspm::enable())" >> "$(R RHOME)/etc/Rprofile.site"'
From then on, inside Positron’s R console, the normal command just works and pulls binaries:
install.packages("tidyverse")
library(tidyverse)


4.3 Fallback: compile from source
Use this route if your Ubuntu release is not covered by r2u, you do not want a system-wide (sudo) install, or a package you need is not in r2u. Compiling the tidyverse from source needs both a C/C++ toolchain and the header files of the system libraries several of its packages link against. Install them all at once:
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y \
  r-base r-base-dev cmake \
  libcurl4-openssl-dev libssl-dev libxml2-dev libfontconfig1-dev \
  libharfbuzz-dev libfribidi-dev libfreetype6-dev libpng-dev \
  libjpeg-dev
(on 24.04 “noble” the JPEG/TIFF library is libtiff6-dev; on 22.04 “jammy” and older it is libtiff5-dev, so append the one matching your release).
Then, still in the terminal, install pak (a modern, fast package manager that also helps resolve these build issues) and use it from the R console:
sudo Rscript -e 'install.packages("pak")'
pak::pak("tidyverse")
library(tidyverse)
Unlike the r2u path (4.2) where plain install.packages() pulls prebuilt binaries, here pak actually compiles from source, but it does the dependency bookkeeping for you and caches the compiled result, so a later reinstallation is quick.

title: Setup your machine for data science with R & Python
text:
5. Install R packages
Open the R console in Positron and run:
install.packages("tidyverse")   # the core data-science collection
On Ubuntu with r2u set up (section 4.2), this command automatically installs Ubuntu binaries, so you do not need pak or the manual toolchain. On macOS/Windows the installer handles everything for you.
A note on the two commands you will meet in this guide:

install.packages() is the R-basics installer. With r2u (+bspm) running it installs Ubuntu binaries, which is why it is the default here.
pak::pak() is an optional third-party package manager with better dependency resolution and caching, and can also install straight from GitHub or a local folder. It does not go through r2u, so on the r2u path it offers no speed advantage. Reach for it when a package is not (yet) on CRAN, or to compile from source as in the fallback (section 4.3).

Verify with:
library(tidyverse)
You should see the package startup message listing dplyr, tidyr, ggplot2, readr, purrr, tibble, stringr, forcats.
By the time of the Reproducible Workflows course you will additionally want:
install.packages(c("janitor", "naniar", "skimr", "renv", "knitr", "rmarkdown", "pins"))
(renv is used for dependency pinning; pins for data pinning; janitor/naniar/skimr feed the data-cleaning and EDA labs. All of these are available as r2u binaries too, so the same plain install.packages() call above works unchanged on the r2u path.)

2.2 The pipe: |>
The pipe |> sends the value on its left into the first argument of the function on its right:

The pipe: top-to-bottom
penguins |>                                        # raw data set
  dplyr::filter(species == "Adelie") |>            # keep only Adelie penguins
  dplyr::mutate(body_mass_kg = body_mass_g / 1000) # compute a new column

Reads: penguins, THEN filter(…). One line per data processing step: easy to comment/read.

The nested equivalent: inside-out
filtered_penguins <- dplyr::filter(penguins, species == "Adelie")
dplyr::mutate(filtered_penguins, body_mass_kg = body_mass_g / 1000)


The pipe keeps your script readable top-to-bottom; the nested alternative reads inside-out. The backbone of data work: one rule, the data always goes first.


3.1 Why plot?
A plot is the fastest way to feel your data. Anscombe’s quartet is the classic proof: four data sets with nearly identical means, variances and correlations, yet plots that look nothing alike.










The four data sets share the same slope, intercept, correlation and means; only the plots tell them apart. A table could not, a hist() of a single column would not, an illustration does.

The lesson. Look at your data before you summarise it: a single well-chosen plot often tells you more than ten summary statistics. This is the heart of Exploratory Data Analysis.



markdown## Why plot? {.inv}

A plot is the fastest way to *feel* your data. Anscombe's quartet is the classic proof: four data sets with nearly identical means, variances and correlations, yet plots that look nothing alike.

::: {.split-2}
```{r}
#| label: anscombe
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4.8
par(bg = "white")                 # opaque white figure so the black ink shows on the dark slide
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(2.5, 2.5, 2, 1), cex = 0.8)
for (i in 1:4) {
  plot(anscombe[, c(2*i - 1, 2*i)], pch = 19, col = "#2E7D6B",
       main = paste0("Dataset ", i))
}
```

The four data sets share the same slope, intercept, correlation and means; only the *plots* tell them apart. A table could not, a `hist()` of a single column would not, an illustration does.

::: {.callout-desc}
**The lesson.** Look at your data before you summarise it: a single well-chosen plot often tells you more than ten summary statistics. This is the heart of *Exploratory Data Analysis*.
:::

An important ggplot2 habit: plots are built from many layers. For example, scatter + a smooth trend:

    data = penguins, 
    mapping = aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g)

    color = "#E8A33D", 
    linewidth = 1
  ) + 
  theme_dark()









































geom_point() and geom_smooth() layer on the same plot, each with its own mapping. This layering is what makes ggplot2 so expressive.
